quickSteps: Confirm the timeline resolution and frame rate
Configure Live Save and project backups
proSteps: Confirm the final deliverables first: landscape or vertical, resolution, frame rate, and HDR or SDR.
Set the timeline frame rate in Project Settings > Master Settings before importing media; Resolve may prevent changes afterward.
For a small SDR project, DaVinci YRGB Color Managed is a practical choice; if requirements are unclear, start with a Rec.709 Gamma 2.4 delivery target.
Place working folders, cache files, proxy media, and gallery stills on a fast drive with sufficient free space.
Enable Live Save, then set the project-backup interval and retention count.
Create Media Pool bins such as 01_MEDIA, 02_AUDIO, 03_GFX, 04_TIMELINES, and 99_EXPORTS.
mistake: Importing media and then changing the timeline frame rate casually can create irreversible timing problems.
doneCheck: The timeline frame rate, resolution, color management, backup settings, and cache locations are confirmed.
proNotes: Frame rate is a project-level decision
Apply the output transform only once

quickSteps: Copy the media and preserve the full card structure
Sync production sound and generate proxy media
proSteps: Copy each camera card in full with its original directory structure; do not copy only the video files, and keep at least two independent copies.
Import on the Media page and check for offline or corrupt clips, unexpected frame rates, and incorrect audio-channel layouts.
Use metadata, clip colors, keywords, and Smart Bins to build a searchable structure.
For dual-system sound, sync by timecode when available; otherwise use waveforms and spot-check the head, middle, and tail.
Generate proxy media when long-GOP or high-resolution footage does not play smoothly. Edit with proxies and use the original media for final output.
Create string-out, select, and reject markers for interviews, narrative work, or documentaries while preserving the source footage.
mistake: Moving source files in Finder takes them offline; move or relink media from within Resolve.
doneCheck: All media is online; sync spot checks pass; scenes and shots are searchable; and two backups exist.
proNotes: Proxy media, optimized media, and render cache are three different tools
Spot-check sync at the head, middle, and tail

quickSteps: Keep only material that advances the cut
Watch the full cut and log issues
proSteps: Create a separate rough-cut timeline instead of repeatedly overwriting the only timeline.
Choose shots according to scene objectives and story progression; do not obsess over transitions at this stage.
Use In and Out points with three-point editing to place useful material quickly.
Address structure, sequences, and pacing first; make only a temporary audio balance sufficient for clarity.
After completing each sequence, play from the end of the previous one to judge whether the emotional handoff works.
Play the entire cut without stopping. Add markers as issues arise, then address them after the screening.
mistake: Grading while you edit can hide structural problems and waste time.
doneCheck: The story is clear from beginning to end, temporary audio is intelligible, and issues are marked by category.
proNotes: A rough cut should be understandable to a first-time viewer
During a full screening, log issues without stopping to make changes

proSteps: Fine-tune edit points around performance and reaction; listen first, then decide when to cut the picture.
Use roll, ripple, slip, and slide trims, and understand which side of the edit each operation changes.
Use a J-cut to bring in the next shot's audio early and an L-cut to carry the previous shot's audio over the cut, softening hard transitions.
Check action matches, eyelines, the 180-degree axis, shot-size changes, and screen direction.
Zoom into the timeline and check for single-frame black gaps, duplicate frames, broken transitions, and stray audio.
Duplicate the timeline before picture lock and label it clearly; log every subsequent change.
mistake: An incorrect ripple trim can shift sync throughout the rest of the program; check the total duration after the edit.
doneCheck: Performance and dialogue flow naturally, no flash frames or gaps remain, and a picture-lock version has been saved.
proNotes: Hold K and tap J or L for slow playback
For the final fine-cut pass, listen without picture once and watch without sound once

quickSteps: Duck music and effects under dialogue
proSteps: Split and label tracks consistently: DX for dialogue, AMB for ambience, SFX for sound effects, and MX for music.
Balance clips with clip gain first, then mix overall levels with track faders; do not stack plug-ins at the outset.
Remove clipped peaks, mouth clicks, and obvious noise; add short crossfades at edits and fill gaps with room tone.
Cut problematic frequencies with EQ before boosting; use compression to control dynamics without flattening dialogue.
Lower music and effects under dialogue, using automation where needed.
Check the mix on headphones and consumer speakers, and watch the meters for clipping.
mistake: Heavy limiting on the main bus can raise the noise floor along with the signal.
doneCheck: Dialogue remains intelligible, edits do not pop, room tone is continuous, and the main output does not clip.
proNotes: Preserve the original sync-sound track
Dialogue clarity depends on spectral separation from the background, not level alone

quickSteps: Confirm input and output color spaces
Open the scopes and make a primary correction
Refine skin tones and local areas
proSteps: Confirm the input color space for each camera format so Log is not treated as Rec.709 and transforms are not applied twice.
Read the Waveform, RGB Parade, and Vectorscope before judging exposure, color balance, and saturation.
Establish exposure with Offset or HDR global controls, then refine with Lift/Gamma/Gain or Curves.
Choose a hero shot as the reference and match other shots within the scene; do not grade every shot in isolation just to make it look attractive.
Keep qualifier keys and Power Windows soft, and check tracked windows for drift.
Separate technical corrections from look nodes; place noise reduction early and sharpening or grain late in the node tree.
Verify the output transform, color-space tags, and highlight range in the actual delivery viewing environment.
mistake: Applying a LUT without color management can clip highlights, introduce a color cast, or duplicate a transform.
doneCheck: Inputs are interpreted correctly, scopes show no unintended clipping, shots within each scene match, and the output transform is applied once.
proNotes: The skin-tone line is a directional reference, not an absolute target
Name and group nodes so the next colorist can understand the grade

quickSteps: Check safe areas and line breaks
proSteps: Define the font, size, leading, outline or background, characters per line, and minimum on-screen duration.
Put dialogue captions on a subtitle track; do not build every caption as a Fusion title.
After automatic transcription, proofread every name, technical term, number, and sentence break.
Ensure subtitles do not cover lower thirds, platform UI, or important picture content.
Check safe areas separately for landscape and vertical deliverables; do not rely on one position to adapt automatically.
Before export, decide whether to burn in subtitles, deliver a sidecar SRT, or provide both.
mistake: Proofreading text without checking timing can make subtitles lead the dialogue or linger too long.
doneCheck: Names and numbers are correct, line breaks are natural, captions do not overlap, and the burn-in or sidecar delivery method is defined.
proNotes: Natural phrase breaks matter more than evenly distributing characters
Check platform safe areas separately for landscape and vertical versions

quickSteps: Log first, then fix in a batch
proSteps: On the first pass, watch the entire program as an audience member and log only story clarity, pacing, and emotional issues.
On the second pass, check for flash frames, black frames, offline media, picture jitter, subtitles, graphics, and copyright notices.
On the third pass, listen without picture and then watch with sound muted to isolate audio and visual continuity problems.
Check the first and last frames, end-card duration, spelling, dates, phone numbers, and brand names.
Check the exported test file on at least two players or devices for gamma differences and A/V sync.
After fixes, reviewing only affected sections is not enough; watch the final master all the way through again.
mistake: Stopping to make each fix as soon as it is found breaks the audience experience of a continuous screening.
doneCheck: No offline media or flash frames remain, subtitles and graphics are correct, and the exported file has been watched in full.
proNotes: Maintain a QC log with timecode, issue, owner, and status
A single black flash warrants frame-by-frame inspection around the edit

quickSteps: Add the job to the render queue
proSteps: Work backward from the delivery requirements to choose the container, codec, resolution, bitrate, audio settings, and color tags.
Confirm whether to render a single clip or individual clips and whether subtitles, alpha, timecode, or handles are required.
Include the project, version, aspect ratio, language, and date in the file name; do not call it only final.mp4.
Render a short test first to check playback, platform compression, and color before rendering the full program.
After adding the job to the render queue, recheck the destination, file name, timeline range, and preset.
Check the final file's duration, resolution, audio tracks, subtitles, color, and full playback.
mistake: Forcing the timeline frame rate to match delivery can introduce duplicate frames or cadence changes.
doneCheck: The render range, destination, codec, audio, and subtitles are correct, and the exported file has passed QC.
proNotes: Keep a high-quality master, then create distribution copies
When players disagree, check color-space tags and the viewing environment first

proSteps: Export a project file or archive and record the Resolve version used.
When using Media Management to collect used media, retain adequate handles and spot-check the relink.
Save high-quality masters, distribution copies, textless masters, split audio stems, subtitles, and key graphics.
Save LUTs, font lists, color-management notes, plug-in inventories, and delivery settings.
Create a README that documents the project contents, folder structure, final timeline, missing items, and recovery steps.
Prove the archive is recoverable by opening it from the archive location and spot-checking shots.
mistake: A DRP without source media does not guarantee long-term recovery.
doneCheck: The project opens, required media is collected, masters and subtitles are complete, and the README and recovery test are finished.
proNotes: An archive should be understandable, verifiable, and recoverable
Keep at least one archive physically separate from the working location

scene: First cuts of interviews, narrative pieces, and promos.
steps: Build the main sequences and key events first
Use In/Out points with F9/F10 for three-point editing
Address only audio problems that prevent understanding
Watch the full cut and log issues with colored markers
risk: Do not spend rough-cut time on final grading or elaborate transitions.
doneCheck: A first-time viewer can follow the cut, and every issue is marked.

steps: Set In and Out points in the Source Viewer
Position the timeline playhead or set a timeline In/Out point
Press F9 to insert or F10 to overwrite
Check track targeting and source audio/video patching
risk: Insert edits shift subsequent material; overwrite edits do not. Choosing the wrong operation can break sync.
doneCheck: The source duration, placement, and target tracks match the intent.

scene: Edits timed to a beat, fitting action to a duration, and B-roll.
steps: Set source In and Out points
Set timeline In and Out points
Press Shift+F11
Choose the appropriate option in the speed-change prompt
risk: Fit to Fill changes playback speed, so it is unsuitable for dialogue that must remain at real speed.
doneCheck: The start and end points align, and the resulting motion speed is acceptable.

steps: Unlink audio and video, or temporarily disable Linked Selection
Extend the incoming clip's audio to the left
Keep the outgoing picture over the incoming audio
Add a short crossfade and listen for continuity in the room tone
risk: Bringing audio in too early can confuse the audience about its source.
doneCheck: The audio leads naturally, and the picture cut does not feel abrupt.

scene: Dialogue reaction shots and interview B-roll.
steps: Set the picture edit point first
Extend the outgoing clip's audio to the right
Cover the continuing dialogue with a reaction shot
Match the ambience across the edit
risk: Carrying the outgoing voice too long can confuse who is speaking.
doneCheck: The audience still knows who is speaking, and the emotion carries naturally.

scene: Replacing shots and finding head or tail handles.
steps: Select the target timeline clip or park the playhead over it
Use Match Frame (F by default)
Review the original media in context in the Source Viewer
Set new In and Out points, then replace the shot
risk: With multicam clips, compound clips, or retimed shots, verify which source level Match Frame opens.
doneCheck: The Source Viewer is parked on the corresponding source frame.

scene: Finding a better performance or B-roll take.
steps: Park the timeline playhead on the frame to use for alignment
Park the Source Viewer on the source frame to align
Press F11 for Replace
Check action alignment and audio tracks
risk: Replace aligns the two playhead frames; an incorrect source playhead position offsets the entire replacement.
doneCheck: Duration remains unchanged, and the key action frames align.

steps: Use clip gain first to bring perceived loudness into line
Remove clipped peaks, mouth clicks, and obvious noise
Add a very short crossfade at each edit
Fill gaps with a separate room-tone recording
Add EQ, compression, and moderate noise reduction only after editing
risk: Too much noise reduction can create underwater or metallic artifacts.
doneCheck: With eyes closed, the edits are inaudible and every word is clear.

steps: Complete the edit at normal speed first
Add retime points
Use Retime Curve to adjust speed and frame timing
Choose the appropriate retime process for slow motion
Check frame by frame for warping and ghosting
risk: Optical Flow can invent bad frames where objects cross, motion blur is heavy, or occlusions occur.
doneCheck: The pacing feels natural, key actions land accurately, and no obvious artifacts remain.

scene: Handheld footage, telephoto shots, and mild mechanical vibration.
steps: Lock the shot duration and retiming first
Analyze with the Stabilizer
Start with Similarity or Translation
Reduce the strength and check the crop
Inspect edges and rolling-shutter wobble frame by frame
risk: More stabilization is not always better; it can exaggerate rolling shutter or make the image float.
doneCheck: Shake is reduced, motion remains natural, and the crop is acceptable.

steps: Confirm the input transform
Read the Waveform and RGB Parade
Set the overall exposure with Offset or Global Exposure
Refine with Lift/Gamma/Gain or HDR zones
Check saturation and channel clipping
risk: Do not crush the blacks to manufacture a 'cinematic' look.
doneCheck: Neutral objects read correctly, the subject is clear, and highlight and shadow placement feels intentional.

steps: Choose a hero shot and grab a still
Enable Split Screen or Reference Wipe
Match exposure first
Then match overall color balance and saturation
Finish with local differences
risk: Match common references and lighting intent, not objects that happen to differ between frames.
doneCheck: Brightness and color do not jump distractingly during continuous playback.

steps: Complete the overall white balance first
Select skin with the Qualifier and soften the key
Constrain the area with a Power Window and track it
Use the skin-tone direction on the Vectorscope as a reference
Review matte edges and motion
risk: The skin-tone line is not an absolute target; preserve differences among complexions and lighting conditions.
doneCheck: Skin looks natural, the key is stable, and the background is not visibly affected.

steps: 01 Noise reduction (when needed)
02 Input / exposure
03 White balance / shot matching
04 Skin / local corrections
05 Look
06 Pre-output trim
Let project color management or a dedicated node handle the output transform consistently
risk: Do not apply the output transform twice through both project-level color management and a CST node.
doneCheck: Nodes are clearly named, and their purpose remains obvious when each node is bypassed.

scene: Lifting a face, darkening a background, or correcting a local color cast.
steps: Create a soft Power Window
Set the shape and feathering on a representative frame
Track forward and backward
Check occlusions and exits from frame
Correct drift with keyframes section by section
risk: A hard-edged or overly bright window looks like a stage spotlight.
doneCheck: At normal playback speed, the window edge is invisible and the track does not drift.

scene: High-ISO footage, lifted shadows, and texture matching.
steps: Apply temporal noise reduction first when needed
Use a small amount of spatial noise reduction for any remaining noise
Complete the primary grade
Add subtle sharpening or Midtone Detail
Finish with film grain to unify the texture
risk: Resolve Studio's noise reduction is processing-intensive; aggressive settings can erase skin texture and slow renders.
doneCheck: Both paused and playing images look natural, without smearing, waxiness, or harsh edges.

scene: After picture lock and before final delivery.
steps: First pass: watch the story without interruption
Second pass: check technical issues and text item by item
Third pass: listen without picture, then watch with sound muted
Log every issue with a timecode
After repairs, watch the entire program again
risk: Fixing as you watch breaks the full-program experience and makes later issues easy to miss.
doneCheck: Every item is closed, and the final file has passed a full-length viewing.

scene: Every project with a formal delivery.
steps: Export a DRP or DRA
Use Media Management to collect used media with handles
Save masters, subtitle files, and split audio stems
Include inventories of LUTs, fonts, and plug-ins
Write a README and perform a spot recovery test
risk: Keeping only the distribution MP4 is not an archive.
doneCheck: The project opens and relinks on another workstation or from a clean path.

steps: Identify the input color space for each camera format
Choose either an RCM or CST workflow
Confirm that the output transform is applied only once
doneCheck: Log, RAW, and Rec.709 media are interpreted correctly.
risk: Combining RCM with a node-based CST can apply the transform twice.
commonMistakes: Applying the output transform in both RCM and a CST

steps: Open the Waveform, RGB Parade, and Vectorscope
Set overall exposure with Offset or HDR controls first
Refine with Lift/Gamma/Gain or Curves
doneCheck: The subject reads clearly, and no channel clips unintentionally.
risk: Crushed blacks do not create a cinematic look.
commonMistakes: Judging only by the display instead of the scopes

steps: Choose a hero shot and grab a still
Match exposure first
Then match overall color balance and saturation
doneCheck: Continuous playback shows no obvious jumps in brightness or color.
risk: Match common references and lighting intent, not different objects within the frame.
commonMistakes: Matching objects that happen to differ between shots
Grading every shot in isolation just to make it look attractive

steps: After balancing the shot, qualify the skin
Soften the key and constrain it with a Power Window
After tracking, check matte edges and motion
doneCheck: Skin looks natural, the key is stable, and the background is unaffected.
risk: The skin-tone line indicates direction; it is not a single target for every complexion.
commonMistakes: Treating the skin-tone line as an absolute target
Using hard qualifier or window edges

steps: Place noise reduction early in the node tree when needed
Keep exposure, shot matching, local corrections, and look nodes separate
Name nodes and compare with them bypassed
doneCheck: The purpose of each layer remains clear when it is bypassed.
risk: Do not mix project-level output management into look nodes.
commonMistakes: Combining technical corrections and the look in one node
Mixing project-level output management into look nodes

steps: Complete the primary grade, then add a small amount of sharpening
Finish with film grain to unify the texture
Check color-space tags, highlights, and the target viewing environment
doneCheck: The image looks natural both playing and paused, and the output tags are correct.
risk: Excessive noise reduction can erase skin texture and slow rendering.
commonMistakes: Overdoing noise reduction creates a waxy look or motion smearing.
Failing to check color-space tags in the target viewing environment

Approximately 8–16 Mb/s; render a short test first

fileChecks: Watch the actual file from start to finish
Verify the file name, version, and date
Verify resolution, frame rate, and AAC audio

Upload a short test and inspect the platform transcode

fileChecks: Watch the actual file from start to finish
Check the 9:16 frame and safe areas
Verify subtitles, audio, and reframed shots
Run a short test on the target platform

Check handles, timecode, retiming, and reframing

Spot-check relinks and the color-management notes

cause: Drive-letter or volume-name changes, moved media, broken proxy paths, or unavailable codecs.
fix: Confirm that the media drive is mounted and its volume name has not changed
In the Media Pool, select the offline clips, then choose Relink Selected Clips
If only proxy media is offline, switch to the originals or relink the proxy media
deep: Check file extensions, camera-original folder structures, OS codec support, and path capitalization.
prevent: Move media from within the project or use Media Management for archives; do not change paths casually in Finder.

cause: Highly compressed long-GOP media, effects, noise reduction, a slow cache drive, or excessive resolution.
fix: Confirm that background rendering is not running and the disk is not full
Set Playback > Timeline Proxy Resolution to Half or Quarter
Generate proxy media; use Render Cache for complex effects
deep: Identify whether decoding, GPU, or disk I/O is the bottleneck; disable noise reduction and other effects one at a time.
prevent: Edit with proxy media and switch back to the original media for final output; keep the render cache on a separate fast drive.

cause: Audio sample-rate mismatches, variable-frame-rate phone footage, incorrect frame-rate interpretation, or a bad sync point.
fix: Confirm the timeline frame rate and clip frame-rate interpretation
Transcode phone VFR footage to a constant-frame-rate mezzanine file first
Compare sync at the head, middle, and tail to distinguish a fixed offset from continuous drift
deep: A fixed offset can be corrected by shifting the clip; continuous drift requires resampling or a slight speed adjustment.
prevent: Use synchronized timecode and consistent sample rates on set, slate each take, and detect VFR phone footage before ingest.

cause: Color-space tags, viewer gamma, display color management, or duplicate/missing output transforms.
fix: Confirm that the output has exactly one Rec.709 transform
Check the export Color Space Tag and Gamma Tag
Compare in a controlled player and on the scopes
deep: First determine whether the file data is wrong or only the display differs.
prevent: Create short test exports and a target-platform test workflow, and document project color management.

cause: Proxy file-name or timecode mismatch, incorrect paths, or delivery settings that force proxy use.
fix: Check proxy paths and metadata in the Media Pool
Disable proxy media, then relink the correct files.
In Advanced Settings on the Deliver page, confirm that Use proxy media is disabled
deep: Spot-check the first frame, duration, frame rate, audio tracks, and timecode against the original media.
prevent: Standardize proxy presets and naming; do not use low-bitrate files from an unknown source.

cause: Corrupt cache files, insufficient cache-drive space, or a node cache that was not invalidated.
fix: Confirm that the cache drive is writable and has free space
Choose Playback > Delete Render Cache > All or Selected Clips
If necessary, change the cache mode and rebuild the cache
deep: Do not delete source media; clear only CacheClip files or manage the cache from Resolve.
prevent: Use a dedicated cache folder, clean it regularly, and never treat cache files as the project archive.

cause: Burn Into Video was not selected, a sidecar subtitle file was not delivered, or the subtitle track is disabled.
fix: On the Deliver page, choose Burn Into Video or export a subtitle file
Confirm that the correct subtitle track is enabled
Render a 20-second test and verify it in the target player
deep: Distinguish among burn-in, embedded, and sidecar subtitle delivery.
prevent: List subtitle mode, language, and file name as separate items in the delivery checklist.

cause: Corrupt frames, plug-ins, Fusion compositions, VRAM, disk space, or encoder problems.
fix: Record the failure timecode and inspect frames around it
Temporarily bypass complex effects and noise reduction to isolate the fault
Render a ProRes or DNxHR mezzanine master first, then transcode the distribution file
deep: A repeatable failure at one frame points to media or effects; a moving failure point more often indicates resource or hardware limits.
prevent: For long-form work, run short tests first and leave ample free space on cache and output drives.

cause: Incorrect bus assignment, muted tracks, Export Audio disabled, or wrong channel mapping.
fix: On the Deliver page, confirm that Export Audio is enabled
In Fairlight, verify track-to-bus routing
Check the bus format and exported channel mapping
deep: For multichannel delivery, verify each bus, track format, and output-file channel mapping.
prevent: Save known-good delivery presets and verify channel mapping in the rendered file.

cause: A one-frame gap between clips, insufficient transition handles, offline frames, or retime-effect boundaries.
fix: Use Up/Down Arrow to jump between edit points
Use Left/Right Arrow to inspect frame by frame
Zoom into the timeline, remove gaps, or adjust transition handles
deep: If the timeline has no gaps, check for corrupt source frames, Optical Flow artifacts, or Fusion boundaries.
prevent: Before picture lock, inspect every edit point and run black-frame detection.

cause: Live Save or backups are disabled, or the only timeline has been overwritten repeatedly.
fix: In Project Manager, right-click the project and open its backups
Restore the latest stable backup and save it as a new version
Check timeline-backup and project-backup locations
deep: Duplicate the recovered project before further work so remaining restore points are not overwritten.
prevent: Use Live Save, project backups, and timeline duplicates at key milestones.

cause: Third-party plug-ins, fonts, LUTs, or DCTLs were not archived with the project.
fix: Read the missing-item warnings and record each name
Install licensed copies of the same versions
If an item cannot be restored, rebuild against the master reference and document any differences
deep: Plug-in version changes can alter the result, so recording only the plug-in name is insufficient.
prevent: Archive font lists, plug-in versions, LUTs/DCTLs, and screenshots of key effect settings.
